extracted.intended_audience: general public and aviation professionals (regulators, airlines, engineers, journalists)
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style informational article documenting the timeline, investigations, regulatory actions, technical changes, and consequences of the Boeing 737 MAX groundings. It summarizes accident findings, certification and return-to-service requirements, and regulatory responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICAO Annex 13 investigation participation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: ICAO regulations Annex 13, 'Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation', defines which states may participate in investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the two MAX accidents the participating states included: the state of occurrence, the state of registration and operator (Indonesia for Lion Air Flight 610; Ethiopia for Flight 302), and the United States as the state of manufacturer and issuer of the type certificate. Participating national transportation safety bureaus and technical assistance providers (e.g., NTSB, NTSC, BEA, Australia, Singapore) are identified per Annex 13.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory grounds for grounding aircraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil aviation authorities may ground an aircraft type over safety concerns when evidence suggests an unsafe condition or similarities between accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the Ethiopian Airlines crash, many civil aviation authorities (beginning with China) grounded the MAX as new evidence revealed accident similarities. Groundings can be ordered independently by national authorities even before other regulators (e.g., FAA) act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency Airworthiness Directive / Continued Airworthiness Notification (EAD/CANIC) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators issue emergency directives requiring changes to manuals, procedures, and inspections when an 'unsafe condition' is identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FAA Emergency airworthiness directive 2018-23-51 and related Continued Airworthiness Notification required revising the aircraft flight manual (AFM) to provide runaway horizontal stabilizer trim procedures when repeated nose‑down trim commands are caused by an erroneously high single AoA sensor. In 2024 the FAA issued an EAD mandating inspection of door plugs on 737 MAX 9s and stated affected aircraft remain grounded until operators complete enhanced inspections (left and right cabin door exit plugs, door components, fasteners) and corrective actions based on findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAA return-to-service / airworthiness certificate preconditions for MAX
rubrics_metrics.description: Before issuing airworthiness certificates and allowing return to service, the FAA stipulated system, maintenance and training requirements and mandated design changes be implemented on each aircraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific FAA requirements included: MCAS design changes (see separate criterion), input from two AoA sensors for MCAS activation, elimination of MCAS's ability to repeatedly activate, allowing pilots to override the system, overhaul of flight control computer architecture to increase redundancy, completion of an AoA sensor system test and a validation test flight for each aircraft, and issuance of airworthiness certificates by the FAA without delegation to Boeing.

rubrics_metrics.name: MCAS design and safety-change requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Design changes to the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS) were required to address hazards identified in accident investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FAA-approved changes included requiring input from two AoA sensors for MCAS activation, eliminating the system's ability to repeatedly activate, and allowing pilots to override the system. Boeing also overhauled the computer architecture of the flight controls to provide greater redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot training and documentation obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots must be trained on MAX-specific failure scenarios and be informed in manuals of systems like MCAS; regulators required new training before pilots may operate the MAX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAA required new simulator training specific to the MAX, including recovering from a simulated MCAS failure. Boeing had previously removed references to MCAS from manuals and argued that simulator time was not needed; regulators later required that AFM/QRH include runaway stabilizer procedures and that operators provide simulator training in addition to computer-based training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer disclosure and transparency expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers are expected to disclose relevant design changes, system functions, and safety analyses to regulators and operators; withholding such information is subject to investigation and penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents that Boeing removed references to MCAS from the FCOM and other manuals and initially did not reveal the system's existence to pilots. Investigations (House, DOJ, Inspector General) criticized Boeing and the FAA for lack of transparency; Boeing settled fraud charges and paid fines related to hiding information from the FAA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization Designation Authorization (ODA) delegation and oversight limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory delegation programs (like the FAA's ODA) grant manufacturers authority to act on the regulator's behalf, but such delegation can be revoked if oversight is weakened or undue pressure is exerted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FAA revoked Boeing's authority to issue airworthiness certificates for individual MAX airplanes and fined Boeing for exerting 'undue pressure' on its designated aircraft inspectors. Post-grounding oversight included limiting delegation and having FAA issue certificates directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational bulletins and non-normal checklist (NNC) integration
rubrics_metrics.description: When a systemic hazard is identified, manufacturers must issue operational bulletins and incorporate procedures into flight manuals and non-normal checklists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Boeing issued an Operations Manual Bulletin (OMB) and a supplementary service bulletin instructing pilots to use existing Runaway Stabilizer Non‑Normal Checklist procedures; the FAA's emergency directive required inclusion of the bulletin information in AFMs and pilot review of the procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production quality, conformity and post-incident inspection requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers must ensure completed products conform to approved designs and are in a condition for safe operation; regulators can audit production and require targeted inspections after in‑service incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the Alaska Airlines Flight 1282 plug blowout, the FAA investigated whether Boeing failed to ensure completed products conformed to approved design, increased oversight of production, and mandated inspections. Airlines found loose bolts and installation issues during mandated inspections of door plug assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident-reporting conventions and causal-factor presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different investigative bodies may present causal factors differently; some list causes without ranking while others identify a primary cause and list contributors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NTSC final report for Lion Air listed nine causal factors and explicitly stated they were not ranked, contrasting with NTSB practice of identifying a primary cause then listing contributing issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quantitative risk assessments in certification oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulators and certification offices review quantitative risk assessments to evaluate the safety implications of design features and certification decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: FAA Seattle Certification Office reviewed a TARAM (Transport Aircraft Risk Assessment Methodology) analysis concluding MCAS design flaws could cause up to 15 future fatal crashes over 30 years if left uncorrected; such analyses influence scrutiny of certification claims and required mitigations.
